heading_path: HydraRNA: a hybrid architecture based fulllength RNA language model
primary_data_source_chunk.heading: Development of HydraRNA
primary_data_source_chunk.text:
HydraRNA: a hybrid architecture based fulllength RNA language model
Results
Development of HydraRNA
HydraRNA is based on a hybrid architecture consisting of both Hydra [18] and multihead attention (MHA) [13] layers (Fig. 1a). It has 12 layers in total. Each layer contains a Hydra module except the 6th and 12th layer, which contains an MHA module. Hydra is  a  natural  bidirectional  extension  of  the  structured  state  space  model  [18]  (Fig.  1b). HydraRNA takes advantages of Hydra's linear scalability of sequence length and high efficiency in in-context learning. The MHA layer was inserted into the stack of Hydra layers  to  further  improve  the  model  quality  as  well  as  to  enhance  the  explainability.
Fig. 1 Overview of HydraRNA. a HydraRNA employs a hybrid architecture with 12 layers. Each layer contains a Hydra module except the 6th and 12th layer, which contains a MHA module, i.e. C = 2,N = 5,M = 1 in this case. b Illustration of Hydra module. c HydraRNA was pretrained on 28.1 million RNAs including both non-coding and protein-coding RNAs using masked language modeling. d Task-specific prediction head was added to the HydraRNA encoder. e Radar plot for overview of prediction performance comparison
Each layer has a hidden state dimension of 1024. HydraRNA was pre-trained on 28 million sequences of non-coding RNAs and protein-coding mRNAs from RNAcentral and NCBI databases (Fig. 1c). Each nucleotide is processed as a single token. A BERT-like random masking strategy was used in the pre-training step. To speed up training, RNA sequences longer than 4096 nt were split into segments of length at most 4096 nt. About 90% of RNAs were pre-trained as full-length  sequences  without  segmentation  (Additional file 1: Figure S1). It took only about 92 h to pre-train HydraRNA on a server with 8  consumer-grade 4090D GPU cards. The time and cost of training were significantly reduced compared to previous RNA LLMs (Additional file 1: Table S1). We conducted several ablation studies to determine the optimal choice of architecture and pre-training  strategy.  More  technical  details  were  provided  in  the  Methods  section.  For  each downstream task, a task-specific prediction head was added to the HydraRNA encoder (Fig. 1d). Unless otherwise specified, a simple MLP predictor with a single 128-dimensional hidden layer was employed for each task. We fully or partially fine-tuned other RNA LLM models using the same approach as we employed for HydrRNA. A radar plot (Fig. 1e) was shown for overview of the prediction performance comparison.

heading_path: HydraRNA: a hybrid architecture based fulllength RNA language model
primary_input_representation_chunk.heading: Random span masked language model
primary_input_representation_chunk.text:
HydraRNA: a hybrid architecture based fulllength RNA language model
Methods
Random span masked language model
The  masking  strategy  used  in  RNA-FM,  RNABERT  [10],  RNA-MSM  [11],  LAMAR [49],  3UTRBERT and UTR-LM was originally from BERT [50], which is essentially at base-level.  Specifically,  15%  of  the  nucleobases  are  randomly  selected  within  an  RNA sequence.  Among  the  selected  tokens,  80%  are  masked,  10%  are  preserved  without any alterations, and the remaining 10% are replaced with other nucleobases. Based on ERNIE,  RNAErnie  introduced  a  motif-aware  multilevel  masking  strategy  to  pre-train the model. It maintained a proportion of 1:1:1 across the three different masking levels (base-level, subsequence-level and motif-level), with the training algorithm randomly selecting  one  strategy  for  each  training  session.  Although  this  motif-aware  masking strategy  could  incorporate  biological  priors  into  the  training  process,  it  may  complicate the training process and biased to the known motif databases. We also noticed that another RNA foundation model, ERNIE-RNA [51] also used ERNIE masking strategy during pre-training.
We  proposed  a  novel  unified  masking  strategy  for  masked  language  modelling, which is called random span masking. In this strategy, multiple span regions (contiguous nucleobase sequences) that covering 15% of the nucleobases are randomly selected. Among  the  selected  nucleobases,  80%  are  masked  with < mask > token,  10%  are  preserved without any alterations, and the remaining 10% are replaced with other nucleobases. This unified masking strategy generalize the classical BERT-like masking strategy to implicitly capture the deeper biological information underling the consecutive region in the whole RNA transcript context, while it also avoid explicitly using biased motif priors. If the mean length of the span masks is set to be 1, it degenerates to the conventional BERT-like masking strategy.

heading_path: HydraRNA: a hybrid architecture based fulllength RNA language model
data_source_chunks.heading: Data for pre-training
data_source_chunks.text:
HydraRNA: a hybrid architecture based fulllength RNA language model
Methods
Data for pre-training
RNA  sequences  from  RNAcentral  database  were  first  filtered  to  include  only  RNAs with length between 18nt and 20,000nt, resulting in 32.5 million RNAs. Redundant and highly  similar  sequences  were  removed  by  using  mmseqs  [53]  with  sequence  identity cutoff at 0.8. 14.4 million RNAs were retained. 58.1 million RNA sequences from NCBI/ RefSeq database were downloaded, which spread across 1,277 species. The transcripts of  different  species  were  downloaded  from    h  t  t  p  s  :  /  /  f  t  p  .  n  c  b  i  .  n  l  m  .  n  i  h  .  g o  v  / g  e n  o  m  e  s /  a l  l /  a n  n  o  t  a  t  i  o  n  _  r  e  l  e  a  s  e  s  /, which contains the products of the NCBI Eukaryotic Genome   A  n n  o  t  a  t  i  o  n Pipeline. The data in this website are organized by taxonomy ID. Redundant and highly similar RefSeq sequences were also removed by using mmseqs with sequence identity  cutoff  at  0.8,  which  results  in  28.07  million  RNAs.  Then  these  42.48  million filtered  sequences from RNAcentral and NCBI were combined and further filtered by mmseq with sequence identity cutoff at 0.5. Here, we did not manually select or discard the transcripts but just used the representative transcripts produced by mmseqs clustering. Finally 28.09 million RNA sequences (including 13.9 million RNAcentral sequences and 14.2 NCBI sequences) were used for pre-training, covering about 51 billion nucleotide tokens. The mean and median length of these RNA is 1811 and 1119 nt, respectively, with 89.7% shorter than 4096 nt. To speed up training, sequences longer than 4096 nt were split into segments of length at most 4096 nt. Each nucleotide is a single token. All 'U' in the sequences were replaced with 'T' . This leads to a vocabulary of standard IUPAC  nucleotide  codes  (A,T,G,C,N,R,Y,K,M,W,S,D,H,V,B).  Special  tokens  that  commonly used in MLM, such as < s >, < pad >, </s >, < unk > and < mask >, were added to the vocabulary. Special token < s > and </s > were added at the start and end of each sequence during pre-training, respectively.
For  the  RNA  secondary  structure  prediction  task,  we  performed  a  second  stage  of pre-training using a curated dataset of non-coding RNAs. Specifically, sequences from bpRNA-1m and archiveII dataset were combined as queries to extract similar sequences from  RNAcentral  dataset  with  sequence  identity  cutoff  of  0.5.  Then  the  retrieved sequences  were  combined  with  the  queries  as  well  as  the  Rfam  dataset.  Next,  highly similar sequences were removed by using mmseqs with sequence identity cutoff at 0.9, which resulted in finally 2.3 million sequences.

input_representation_chunks.heading: Development of HydraRNA
input_representation_chunks.text:
HydraRNA: a hybrid architecture based fulllength RNA language model
Results
Development of HydraRNA
HydraRNA is based on a hybrid architecture consisting of both Hydra [18] and multihead attention (MHA) [13] layers (Fig. 1a). It has 12 layers in total. Each layer contains a Hydra module except the 6th and 12th layer, which contains an MHA module. Hydra is  a  natural  bidirectional  extension  of  the  structured  state  space  model  [18]  (Fig.  1b). HydraRNA takes advantages of Hydra's linear scalability of sequence length and high efficiency in in-context learning. The MHA layer was inserted into the stack of Hydra layers  to  further  improve  the  model  quality  as  well  as  to  enhance  the  explainability.
Fig. 1 Overview of HydraRNA. a HydraRNA employs a hybrid architecture with 12 layers. Each layer contains a Hydra module except the 6th and 12th layer, which contains a MHA module, i.e. C = 2,N = 5,M = 1 in this case. b Illustration of Hydra module. c HydraRNA was pretrained on 28.1 million RNAs including both non-coding and protein-coding RNAs using masked language modeling. d Task-specific prediction head was added to the HydraRNA encoder. e Radar plot for overview of prediction performance comparison
Each layer has a hidden state dimension of 1024. HydraRNA was pre-trained on 28 million sequences of non-coding RNAs and protein-coding mRNAs from RNAcentral and NCBI databases (Fig. 1c). Each nucleotide is processed as a single token. A BERT-like random masking strategy was used in the pre-training step. To speed up training, RNA sequences longer than 4096 nt were split into segments of length at most 4096 nt. About 90% of RNAs were pre-trained as full-length  sequences  without  segmentation  (Additional file 1: Figure S1). It took only about 92 h to pre-train HydraRNA on a server with 8  consumer-grade 4090D GPU cards. The time and cost of training were significantly reduced compared to previous RNA LLMs (Additional file 1: Table S1). We conducted several ablation studies to determine the optimal choice of architecture and pre-training  strategy.  More  technical  details  were  provided  in  the  Methods  section.  For  each downstream task, a task-specific prediction head was added to the HydraRNA encoder (Fig. 1d). Unless otherwise specified, a simple MLP predictor with a single 128-dimensional hidden layer was employed for each task. We fully or partially fine-tuned other RNA LLM models using the same approach as we employed for HydrRNA. A radar plot (Fig. 1e) was shown for overview of the prediction performance comparison.

data_source_sections.heading: Data for pre-training
data_source_sections.text:
RNA  sequences  from  RNAcentral  database  were  first  filtered  to  include  only  RNAs with length between 18nt and 20,000nt, resulting in 32.5 million RNAs. Redundant and highly  similar  sequences  were  removed  by  using  mmseqs  [53]  with  sequence  identity cutoff at 0.8. 14.4 million RNAs were retained. 58.1 million RNA sequences from NCBI/ RefSeq database were downloaded, which spread across 1,277 species. The transcripts of  different  species  were  downloaded  from    h  t  t  p  s  :  /  /  f  t  p  .  n  c  b  i  .  n  l  m  .  n  i  h  .  g o  v  / g  e n  o  m  e  s /  a l  l /  a n  n  o  t  a  t  i  o  n  \_  r  e  l  e  a  s  e  s  /, which contains the products of the NCBI Eukaryotic Genome   A  n n  o  t  a  t  i  o  n Pipeline. The data in this website are organized by taxonomy ID. Redundant and highly similar RefSeq sequences were also removed by using mmseqs with sequence identity  cutoff  at  0.8,  which  results  in  28.07  million  RNAs.  Then  these  42.48  million filtered  sequences from RNAcentral and NCBI were combined and further filtered by mmseq with sequence identity cutoff at 0.5. Here, we did not manually select or discard the transcripts but just used the representative transcripts produced by mmseqs clustering. Finally 28.09 million RNA sequences (including 13.9 million RNAcentral sequences and 14.2 NCBI sequences) were used for pre-training, covering about 51 billion nucleotide tokens. The mean and median length of these RNA is 1811 and 1119 nt, respectively, with 89.7% shorter than 4096 nt. To speed up training, sequences longer than 4096 nt were split into segments of length at most 4096 nt. Each nucleotide is a single token. All 'U' in the sequences were replaced with 'T' . This leads to a vocabulary of standard IUPAC  nucleotide  codes  (A,T,G,C,N,R,Y,K,M,W,S,D,H,V,B).  Special  tokens  that  commonly used in MLM, such as < s >, < pad >, </s >, < unk > and < mask >, were added to the vocabulary. Special token < s > and </s > were added at the start and end of each sequence during pre-training, respectively.

For  the  RNA  secondary  structure  prediction  task,  we  performed  a  second  stage  of pre-training using a curated dataset of non-coding RNAs. Specifically, sequences from bpRNA-1m and archiveII dataset were combined as queries to extract similar sequences from  RNAcentral  dataset  with  sequence  identity  cutoff  of  0.5.  Then  the  retrieved sequences  were  combined  with  the  queries  as  well  as  the  Rfam  dataset.  Next,  highly similar sequences were removed by using mmseqs with sequence identity cutoff at 0.9, which resulted in finally 2.3 million sequences.
